% Generated by experiments/build_vldb.py; edit main.tex/shared inputs.
Volume Under the Surface (VUS) averages time-series anomaly-detection areas
over score thresholds and tolerance widths. We reduce computation along both
axes while preserving a pinned metric definition. First, thresholds outside
the maximum anomaly support contribute analytically integrable ROC rectangles
and zero PR area. Sorting support scores and counting remaining scores yields
exact scalar VUS-ROC and VUS-PR in
$O(n\log(Q+1)+(L+1)Q)$ time and $O(n+Q)$ memory, where $Q$ is the expanded
support size and $L$ the largest width. Support restriction and cumulative
sums are prior techniques; our reduction eliminates inactive threshold events.
Second, expanded-interval merge events partition the width range into regions
with ordered ROC coordinates. A probability-box expectation bound encloses PR
without assuming monotone PR area. Adaptive refinement bounds the discrete
width average to a requested half-width in real arithmetic; the float64
implementation is numerically audited, not a directed-rounding certificate.
Experiments use \NumSeries{} public series and \NumScores{} released score
vectors. Against released fast-VUS computing PR only, the paired ROC/PR
evaluator has median speedups of $8.38\times$ and $4.55\times$ on two CPU systems.
Against the fastest tested comparator, including dense methods, the medians
are $2.04\times$ and $1.35\times$; Sparse VUS is slower or equal in 209 and
574 of 2,100 cases, respectively.
Width refinement evaluates fewer curves but is often slower at tight tolerances.
Incremental PR racing gives median speedups at width 300, yet increases the
sum of per-task median latencies on both machines; both extensions remain optional.
The reference's 250-threshold approximation changes 84 of 2,100 PR pair
orders; 75 and 74 persist after two fixed padding interventions.
The results distinguish exact-integration gains from the cost of
error-bounded width reduction.
